accept: match cuisine styles not just premium serve in wine glasses train staff
range of styles glassware education
ans: Choose by style range (crisp junmai to aromatic daiginjo to aged koshu) rather than grade prestige; serve in wine glasses at correct temperature; train the floor to pair it with non-Japanese food

q: Fitou: what was its historical first, what is odd about its shape on the map, and what must be in the bottle?
accept: first languedoc red aoc in 1948, two zones split by corbieres, carignan and grenache reds
1948 first red appellation of the languedoc, maritime and mountain enclaves, blended red only
two non-contiguous zones inside corbieres, maritime limestone and inland schist, reds from carignan grenache syrah mourvedre
fitou 1948, maritime and haut fitou separated by corbieres, red blends with compulsory ageing
ans: Fitou was the Languedoc's first appellation for red wine, granted in 1948 — decades before its neighbours. It is not one block but two separate zones with Corbières lying between them: Fitou Maritime, on clay-limestone by the sea around Fitou and Leucate, and the upper or mountain Fitou, on schist inland around Tuchan and Villeneuve-les-Corbières, higher, cooler and later-ripening. It is red only, blended, built on Carignan and Grenache Noir with Syrah and Mourvèdre, and must be aged — around nine months — before release. The same vineyards are entitled to Rivesaltes, so growers can declare a fortified wine from the same land.
exp: Fitou is the counterexample to the story that the Languedoc had no quality appellations before the 1980s — it had one, and it was largely wasted on co-operative bulk for forty years. The split geography matters in tasting: maritime Fitou is warmer, rounder and earlier, mountain Fitou darker and firmer. The overlap with Rivesaltes is the detail that separates a prepared candidate from a memorised one.
